The neck is commonly maple or mahogany, and the fretboard Brazilian rosewood, Indian rosewood or ebony. The top, sides and back are made of wood, the top commonly spruce, mahogany, rosewood, maple or ebony, and it may be solid or laminated. The tuning pegs are usually plastic and metal, or wood and metal; the nut and saddle may be plastic, camel bone, cow bone, synthetic resin or metal; the bridge is usually a hardwood; the bridge pins are usually plastic or ebony. In pop, rock, blues, folk and flamenco it is often treated as the main instrument; the steel-strung folk guitar is mostly used to accompany songs, or by a singer playing alone. The electric guitar is usually paired with the drum kit, the bass and voices, and appears in rock, blues, jazz and pop; it has shaped subgenres such as heavy metal and punk. Fingerstyle playing mixes classical and folk technique with some from the electric guitar. The guitar is also heard in fado, jota, ska, mariachi, funk, reggae, soul, disco, new wave, new age, adult contemporary and pop, and now and then appears as a sample in hip-hop, dubstep or trap.

Proposed origins include the ancient Greek kithara, the long-necked lutes of Mesopotamia and the Coptic lutes of ancient Egypt; the earliest relief that looks like a guitar is found at a Hittite site more than three thousand years old. From the twelfth century a range of chordophones appeared in Europe: the gittern in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the vihuela in the fifteenth and sixteenth, and from the middle of the sixteenth century the popular five-course baroque guitar. In the later eighteenth century German makers moved to six single strings, and in the middle of the nineteenth century the Spanish luthier Torres enlarged the body. The electric guitar was patented in 1937, and from the 1960s to the 1970s solid bodies dominated the market.

A wooden guitar is amplified by its hollow soundbox, and the volume depends on the plucking, the strumming, the pick and the vibration of the top; an electric guitar turns the string motion into an electronic signal through pickups, amplifies it through an amplifier, and can change its timbre with effects. Compared with the lute, another chordophone, the modern guitar usually has frets, commonly six strings, and can reach a much greater volume through its pickups.

The guitar is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-5-6. It usually has frets and commonly six or twelve strings, though seven-, eight- and nine-string guitars also exist; it consists of a head, a neck and a body. It is held flat against the body, plucked or strummed with the dominant hand while the other hand stops the strings; a pick may also be used. The wooden guitar is amplified by its hollow soundbox, the electric guitar by pickups and an amplifier. Players use it in pop, rock, blues, folk and flamenco, and in classical music for solos and duos, or to accompany chamber music and the orchestra.

The dominant hand plucks or strums with the fingers or a pick, while the fingers of the other hand press the strings onto the frets; the classical guitar is mostly played fingerstyle, string by string, and the steel-strung folk guitar is often used to accompany a song, or by a singer playing alone. A beginner can first bring the strings up to tension with the tuning pegs, then practise coordinating the two hands, so that the strings' vibration reaches the ear through the hollow body, or through the pickups and the amplifier.
